source.title: Monosemanticity in Recommender Systems
source.authors: Yagel Alfasi; Eden Rzezak; Eadan Schechter

record.tranche_reason: Applies a Matryoshka sparse autoencoder as a post-hoc interpretability tool for recommender embeddings and reports its performance and interventions. It does not test the claim versions about superposition, capacity competition, LLM features, or canonical SAE units.
record.gate_note: The paper reports semantic-coherence measurements and causal interventions on MSAE neurons in a recommender model; these findings do not measure feature overlap, near-orthogonality, capacity competition, or any of the LLM-specific versions. The SAE-versus-MSAE recommendation metrics assess recommendation fidelity, not the claim, so they are not rows. The reported LLM-generated labels are qualitative analysis, not evidence that SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical.
record.test_reason: The study applies a Matryoshka SAE as an interpretability tool to 20-dimensional matrix-factorization item embeddings of a recommender. It reports label coherence, a monosemanticity score and intervention effects on recommendations. It does not measure feature overlap, near-orthogonality, capacity competition, alternative causes of polysemanticity, or feature dimensionality. The system is not an LLM, so V4 does not apply. No row bears on any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also claim the MSAE incurs no measurable cost to recommendation fidelity versus a plain SAE (AUC 0.7754 vs 0.7685; top-10 overlap 87.5%). They frame the interventions as steering recommendations in a controllable and interpretable way.
record.recipe_differences: The paper applies a post-hoc Matryoshka sparse autoencoder to matrix-factorization item embeddings and evaluates semantic labels and recommendation interventions; it does not reproduce the original toy-network superposition method.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported intervention response varies with activation scaling; the paper describes a consistent directional trend over scaling factors 2–16. The MSAE also uses ordered prefix sizes {5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40, 45, 50}.

fits_no_version.finding: In a 50-latent MSAE on 20-d recommender item embeddings, later-indexed latents received more specific LLM labels than early ones, with higher monosemanticity scores on average.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Matryoshka SAEs on recommender embeddings order latents from broad to specific concepts.

fits_no_version.finding: Scaling six women-associated MSAE latents shifted women-associated recommendations by about 1 percentage point. List overlap stayed 0.97 and KL was about 0.07.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE latents on recommender embeddings act as weak causal levers on recommendation composition.

fits_no_version.finding: N3 had a coherent women's-apparel label but among the lowest MS scores (0.076).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Embedding-geometry coherence and label coherence of SAE latents can dissociate.

record.problems: Evidence is from one dataset and domain, with a 50-dimensional MSAE dictionary and interventions on a random sample of 50 users. Semantic labels were generated by Claude Opus 4.5 without reported human validation. The paper notes that the monosemanticity score is an indirect measure of human-perceived interpretability; intervention changes in aggregate percentages were small. No uncertainty estimates are reported.
record.rows_left_out: The study's SAE-versus-MSAE recommendation metrics and top-10 overlap comparison in Section 5.1 were left out because they compare reconstruction fidelity rather than measuring the claim's feature geometry or capacity account. Entropy values in Table 3 were also left out because the paper reports them as nearly unchanged and they do not directly measure the claim versions.

untested.parts: No toy model, no feature-overlap geometry, no sparsity-dependent transition.
No test of capacity competition or of whether important features get dedicated dimensions.
No test of non-capacity causes of polysemantic neurons.
Not an LLM. The study never establishes that the MF embeddings hold more features than dimensions, only that an SAE yields labelable units.
No test of completeness, stability across seeds or sizes, or canonicality of SAE features. LLM labels and interventions only.
No comparison of 1-D directions with multi-dimensional features.

record.verdict_notes: Both SAEs were tuned by Optuna to maximise mean MS, the same metric then reported, which is a selection effect. Gender neurons were chosen from LLM labels. Interventions used 50 users, with no uncertainty estimates. The paper cites superposition only as background motivation for SAEs.

versions.untested_parts: No test of toy-model superposition, feature overlap geometry, or a sparsity-dependent transition.
No test of capacity competition, feature importance, or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions.
No test of alternative causes of polysemantic neurons.
The study analyzes a recommender system, not LLMs, and does not test feature distribution across LLM neurons or SAE recovery in LLMs.
Semantic labels and causal effects do not establish that SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical units.
No comparison of one-dimensional feature directions with multidimensional features.

rows.subject: MSAE on Amazon Fashion MF item embeddings
rows.size_stated: MF embedding dimension 20; MSAE hidden dimension 50
rows.operation_detail: Computed the monosemanticity score for MSAE neurons using item-embedding cosine similarity.
rows.value: Scores range from approximately 0.075 to 0.201; the paper describes clusters at 0.08–0.11 and 0.16–0.19.
rows.note: The paper says top scores were N41 (0.201), N44 (0.196), N43 (0.192), N40 (0.188), and N36 (0.183), and the lowest were N3 (0.076), N1 (0.077), and N0 (0.079). This measures item-set coherence, not feature-direction overlap.

rows.subject: MSAE on Amazon Fashion MF item embeddings
rows.size_stated: MF embedding dimension 20; MSAE hidden dimension 50
rows.operation_detail: Grouped LLM-generated neuron labels by dictionary index.
rows.value: Neurons 0–21 received broad labels such as Clothing, Shoes & Jewelry, without consistent subcategory specialization.
rows.note: Qualitative labels were generated by Claude Opus 4.5.

rows.subject: MSAE on Amazon Fashion MF item embeddings
rows.size_stated: MF embedding dimension 20; MSAE hidden dimension 50
rows.operation_detail: Grouped LLM-generated neuron labels by dictionary index.
rows.value: Neurons 22–35 showed mild demographic focus and partial alignment with gendered product categories.
rows.note: Qualitative labels were generated by Claude Opus 4.5.

rows.subject: MSAE on Amazon Fashion MF item embeddings
rows.size_stated: MF embedding dimension 20; MSAE hidden dimension 50
rows.operation_detail: Grouped LLM-generated neuron labels by dictionary index.
rows.value: Neurons 36–49 had more differentiated labels, including women’s apparel subcategories, footwear types, and accessory segments.
rows.note: Qualitative labels were generated by Claude Opus 4.5.
rows.check: The paper says the gender axis appears exclusively among higher-indexed neurons, yet the set includes N3 (index 3). This internal inconsistency weakens the gradient claim in r2–r4.

rows.subject: MSAE on Amazon Fashion MF item embeddings
rows.size_stated: MF embedding dimension 20; MSAE hidden dimension 50
rows.operation_detail: Compared the label assigned to N3 with its activation-weighted item-embedding similarity score.
rows.measure: Relationship between label coherence and MS
rows.value: N3 received a women’s apparel label but had an MS score of 0.076, among the lowest; the paper says its activating items were geometrically dispersed in MF embedding space.
rows.note: The authors distinguish geometric coherence from the interpretability of the generated label.
